summary:
LunaNav is a free web app that shows when the Sun and the Earth are above the real terrain horizon at NASA’s nine candidate Artemis landing regions near the lunar south pole.

Near the pole the Sun stays a few degrees above the horizon, so a single ridge can hide it for days. At the Malapert Massif point, the longest stretch without Sun in January 2027 is 9.8 days. Sunlight decides power and warmth, and a view of Earth decides direct communication, so a flat horizon gives the wrong answer.

We built the skyline from NASA LOLA terrain data at 80 m per pixel, tracing it out to 150 km from each observation point, and took Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons. Our directions match Horizons to within 0.01°.

The app ranks all nine regions for 2027, lets you stand at each point in 3D, and compares two regions over a week to a year. It runs in any browser, in English and Arabic, and states its limits on screen.
details:
What it does

LunaNav shows when the Sun and the Earth are above the real terrain horizon at NASA’s nine candidate Artemis landing regions near the lunar south pole. Near the pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so one ridge can hide it for days. Sunlight decides power and warmth, and a view of Earth decides direct communication. A flat horizon gives the wrong answer, so LunaNav uses the measured terrain.

The app has three views:

  • Orbit: a 3D Moon built from NASA imagery and terrain, with the nine regions, live Sun and Earth readings, and a ranking of all nine for 2027 by sunlight, Earth visibility and longest darkness.
  • Surface: you stand at the observation point, 2 m above the ground, and see the Sun and the Earth against the measured skyline. You can turn to face either one and run time forward.
  • Analysis: compare two regions over a week to a year. It shows the share of time with Sun and with Earth, a timeline you can inspect minute by minute, the full horizon with both paths, stored energy needed for a chosen load, and the longest gap without Earth. A “Launch delayed?” button re-runs the same site at a later date. Results export to CSV, and every comparison can be shared as a link.

How it works

  1. Terrain: the NASA LOLA height map of the south pole (LDEM_80S_80M, 80 m per pixel).
  2. Skyline: from 2 m above each observation point we trace rays out to 150 km in every direction.
  3. Positions: Sun and Earth directions come from NASA/JPL Horizons, hourly from July 2026 to December 2028, interpolated between hours.
  4. Answer: a body counts as visible when its centre is above the skyline.

We checked the results ourselves. Our Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to within 0.01° at all nine points. Terrain heights match LROC QuickMap within 3 m, and sunlight matches QuickMap in 15 of 18 checks. A button in the app re-checks any moment live against Horizons.

Benefits and intended impact

LunaNav gives students, teachers, outreach teams and anyone following Artemis a quick, checkable first look at a hard geometric idea. One example from the app: over 30 days from 1 January 2027, Malapert Massif and Nobile Rim 1 get almost the same sunlight (67.4% and 67.1%), but Earth is in view 100% of the time at Malapert and 62% at Nobile Rim 1. Two sites that look the same for power are very different for communication. LunaNav is a learning and first-look tool, not a mission-planning system.

Tools

TypeScript, React, Three.js with React Three Fiber, Vite and Zustand for the web app. Python to prepare the NASA data. Vitest and Playwright for automated tests. Recorded narration made with ElevenLabs. Hosted on Vercel. No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser on a computer or phone, with no install and no account.

What makes it creative

It opens with the answer, a ranking of all nine regions, instead of a blank map. You can stand on the surface and see the exact ridge that blocks the Sun. The launch-delay button asks the planner’s real question: what if we land two weeks later?

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every number comes from open NASA data, and we test it against Horizons and QuickMap. Automated checks run on the science, the data, the interface and the shared links.
  • Honesty: the app states its limits on screen. It uses one observation point per region and 80 m terrain traced to 150 km, power and communication figures are estimates from geometry, and LunaNav is not a NASA product.
  • Access: the full interface and a recorded voice guide with captions are available in English and Arabic, with a right-to-left layout. It works on phones and from the keyboard.
